validation.note: Generated structured draft records; numeric-entry and complex-format keys require clinical/editorial completion before production exam use.

items.title: A client using home oxygen asks whether smoking near an open window is safe. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Explain that smoking is prohibited near oxygen; keep oxygen away from flames/heat and post no-smoking signage.
items.rationale: Oxygen accelerates combustion and creates severe fire risk.

items.title: A client with advanced illness has distressing dyspnea despite oxygen saturation 93%. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Assess distress and reversible causes, use positioning/fan and prescribed opioid for air hunger, and align care with goals.
items.rationale: Dyspnea is subjective; opioids can relieve air hunger even when oxygen saturation is not severely low.

items.title: A competent client with a valid advance directive refuses a proposed treatment; family demands it. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Respect the client's informed decision, clarify goals, notify care team, and document discussion.
items.rationale: A competent adult's informed choices guide care; family preference does not override autonomy.

items.title: A client scheduled for surgery says they do not understand the procedure after the surgeon left. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client scheduled for surgery says they do not understand the procedure after the surgeon left.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Pause preparation and contact the surgeon to provide further explanation; the nurse witnesses consent and assesses voluntariness/understanding.
items.rationale: The procedural provider is responsible for explaining risks, benefits, and alternatives; consent must be informed.

items.title: A stable client needs routine vital signs while another client has new chest pain. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A stable client needs routine vital signs while another client has new chest pain.|response:Delegate routine vital signs for the stable client to qualified assistive personnel and personally assess the client with chest pain.|rationale:Unstable/new symptoms require RN assessment; predictable tasks for stable clients may be delegated with follow-up.
items.rationale: Unstable/new symptoms require RN assessment; predictable tasks for stable clients may be delegated with follow-up.

items.title: A confused client repeatedly attempts to climb out of bed; family asks for restraints. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Restraint safety|priority:Assess causes and use least-restrictive alternatives first; if restraint is necessary, follow order, monitoring, release, and documentation requirements.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Restraints are last resort and require ongoing assessment and legal/policy safeguards.

items.title: A nurse discovers that a client received twice the prescribed insulin dose. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Medication error|actions:Assess glucose and symptoms immediately, notify provider, initiate hypoglycemia monitoring/treatment, and report per policy.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Patient assessment and prevention of harm take priority over blame; insulin overdose can cause delayed hypoglycemia.

items.title: A caller claiming to be a client's employer asks for the client's diagnosis. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A caller claiming to be a client's employer asks for the client's diagnosis.|priority:Do not disclose protected information without valid authorization; verify identity and follow privacy policy.
items.rationale: Health information may be shared only with authorized persons and for permitted purposes.

items.title: A conscious client with diabetes is diaphoretic and has glucose 48 mg/dL. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: The 15-15 approach treats an alert client able to swallow; altered consciousness requires glucagon/IV dextrose.

items.title: A chronic wound has purulent drainage, spreading erythema, fever, and increasing pain. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Local wound deterioration with fever may indicate spreading infection or sepsis.

items.title: A client with a central venous catheter develops rigors during infusion and fever. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Stop infusion if clinically indicated, assess stability, notify provider, obtain paired cultures as ordered, and follow line infection protocol.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Rigors during infusion raise concern for bloodstream infection and require prompt evaluation.

items.title: A client with sodium 118 mEq/L develops headache, confusion, and a seizure. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Protect airway and safety, notify emergency team, and anticipate carefully controlled hypertonic saline when indicated with frequent sodium checks.
items.rationale: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia causes cerebral edema; correction must be controlled to avoid osmotic demyelination.

items.title: A client with malignancy has calcium 14.2 mg/dL, constipation, weakness, and confusion. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Hypercalcemia|actions:Initiate prescribed isotonic IV hydration, monitor ECG/renal function, and prepare ordered calcium-lowering therapy.|evaluation:Severe hypercalcemia causes neurologic, renal, and cardiac effects; hydration supports renal calcium excretion.
items.rationale: Severe hypercalcemia causes neurologic, renal, and cardiac effects; hydration supports renal calcium excretion.

items.title: After thyroidectomy, a client reports perioral tingling and has carpopedal spasm. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Assess airway and calcium, notify provider, and prepare IV calcium gluconate for symptomatic hypocalcemia.
items.rationale: Parathyroid injury can cause acute hypocalcemia and tetany; laryngospasm is a serious risk.

items.title: A client with untreated hyperthyroidism has fever 40°C, HR 160/min, agitation, and diarrhea. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Activate emergency response, provide cooling and cardiac monitoring, and administer prescribed beta blocker, antithyroid medication, and supportive therapy.
items.rationale: Thyroid storm is life-threatening thyrotoxicosis with hyperthermia and cardiovascular instability.

items.title: An older adult with hypothyroidism is hypothermic, bradycardic, hypotensive, and obtunded. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Support airway/ventilation and circulation, initiate emergency care, and anticipate IV thyroid hormone and cautious warming as prescribed.
items.rationale: Severe hypothyroidism can cause life-threatening hypometabolism and respiratory/circulatory failure.

items.title: A client with Addison disease has vomiting, abdominal pain, BP 76/42 mm Hg, sodium 126, and potassium 6.0. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client with Addison disease has vomiting, abdominal pain, BP 76/42 mm Hg, sodium 126, and potassium 6.0.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Escalate immediately, administer prescribed IV hydrocortisone and isotonic fluids, and monitor glucose/electrolytes.
items.rationale: Adrenal crisis causes shock and electrolyte disturbance; prompt steroid and fluid replacement are essential.

items.title: A client with small-cell lung cancer has sodium 122 mEq/L, low serum osmolality, and concentrated urine. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client with small-cell lung cancer has sodium 122 mEq/L, low serum osmolality, and concentrated urine.|response:Institute prescribed fluid restriction, monitor neurologic status and sodium, and use hypertonic saline only for severe symptoms as ordered.|rationale:Excess ADH causes water retention and dilutional hyponatremia; correction requires close monitoring.
items.rationale: Excess ADH causes water retention and dilutional hyponatremia; correction requires close monitoring.

items.title: A client with peripheral neuropathy has a painless blister under the forefoot. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Diabetes foot care|priority:Inspect feet daily, avoid self-treatment of lesions, use properly fitted footwear, and arrange prompt foot-care evaluation.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Neuropathy masks injury; early evaluation prevents ulceration and infection.

items.title: A client taking methotrexate reports fever and mouth ulcers. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Rheumatoid arthritis medication|actions:Hold dose pending urgent prescriber review, obtain CBC/liver/renal assessment as ordered, and screen for infection/toxicity.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Methotrexate can cause myelosuppression and mucositis; fever may indicate serious infection.

items.title: A client with lupus has new edema, hypertension, proteinuria, and rising creatinine. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client with lupus has new edema, hypertension, proteinuria, and rising creatinine.|priority:Notify provider promptly, monitor renal function and BP, and anticipate evaluation for lupus nephritis.
items.rationale: Proteinuria and renal impairment suggest organ involvement requiring prompt treatment.

items.title: An older adult taking long-term glucocorticoids has low bone density. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Glucocorticoids increase fracture risk; multifactorial prevention is required.

items.title: A client with Parkinson disease coughs during meals and has a wet voice afterward. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Cough and wet voice suggest aspiration; swallowing assessment guides safe nutrition.

items.title: A client with myasthenia gravis develops weak cough, dysphagia, and declining vital capacity. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Escalate to critical care, assess respiratory mechanics and airway protection, and prepare ventilatory support.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Bulbar and respiratory muscle weakness can progress to respiratory failure.

items.title: A client has ascending weakness and declining forced vital capacity after a respiratory infection. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Notify critical care team, monitor respiratory function and autonomic instability, and prepare for ventilatory support and IVIG/plasma exchange.
items.rationale: Respiratory failure and dysautonomia are major threats in Guillain-Barré syndrome.

items.title: A client with MS reports transient worsening of weakness after a hot shower. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Multiple sclerosis heat sensitivity|actions:Recommend cooling strategies, avoiding overheating, pacing activity, and reporting new persistent neurologic deficits.|evaluation:Heat can temporarily worsen conduction in demyelinated nerves; persistent changes require evaluation.
items.rationale: Heat can temporarily worsen conduction in demyelinated nerves; persistent changes require evaluation.

items.title: A client rescued from an enclosed fire has facial burns, soot in sputum, and hoarseness. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Activate airway response early, administer high-concentration oxygen, and prepare for early intubation assessment.
items.rationale: Airway edema can progress rapidly after inhalation injury; early airway control may be necessary.

items.title: A client has small entry and exit burns after high-voltage exposure and reports palpitations. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Ensure scene safety, obtain ECG and cardiac monitoring, assess deep tissue injury and rhabdomyolysis, and arrange urgent evaluation.
items.rationale: External burns underestimate deep injury; dysrhythmias and muscle damage may occur.

items.title: An older adult found outdoors has core temperature 32°C, confusion, and shivering. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Handle gently, remove wet clothing, initiate controlled rewarming, monitor cardiac rhythm, and avoid rough movement.
items.rationale: Moderate hypothermia can cause dysrhythmias; gentle handling and controlled rewarming reduce risk.

items.title: A rescued swimmer is coughing, hypoxemic, and has crackles despite being awake. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A rescued swimmer is coughing, hypoxemic, and has crackles despite being awake.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Support oxygenation and ventilation, monitor for pulmonary edema, and arrange emergency evaluation and observation.
items.rationale: Respiratory complications may evolve after submersion even when the client is initially alert.

items.title: A client presents after a suspected venomous snakebite with progressive swelling and pain. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client presents after a suspected venomous snakebite with progressive swelling and pain.|response:Keep client calm and limb immobilized at heart level, remove constricting items, mark swelling, and contact poison control/prepare antivenom assessment.|rationale:Avoid tourniquets, cutting, suction, or ice; serial assessment guides antivenom need.
items.rationale: Avoid tourniquets, cutting, suction, or ice; serial assessment guides antivenom need.

items.title: A child may have swallowed household drain cleaner and is drooling. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Poisoning—caustic ingestion|priority:Do not induce vomiting or attempt neutralization; protect airway and contact poison control/emergency services immediately.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Caustic agents cause further injury if vomited or chemically neutralized; airway and specialist guidance are priorities.

items.title: A farm worker has miosis, salivation, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, and muscle fasciculations. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Organophosphate exposure|actions:Use appropriate PPE/decontamination, support airway, and prepare atropine and pralidoxime per protocol.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Cholinergic excess causes life-threatening bronchorrhea and bradycardia; protect rescuers from secondary exposure.

items.title: A toddler may have ingested multiple iron tablets and now has vomiting and abdominal pain. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A toddler may have ingested multiple iron tablets and now has vomiting and abdominal pain.|priority:Contact poison control and emergency services, obtain serum iron/acid-base assessment as ordered, and prepare deferoxamine if indicated.
items.rationale: Iron poisoning can cause severe GI injury, shock, and metabolic toxicity; early specialist treatment matters.

items.title: A client has tinnitus, tachypnea, vomiting, and mixed respiratory alkalosis/metabolic acidosis after overdose. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Salicylate toxicity causes characteristic tinnitus and mixed acid-base disturbance; serum levels and pH guide care.

items.title: A runner has heavy sweating, dizziness, nausea, and temperature 38.2°C but remains oriented. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Heat exhaustion usually preserves mental status; altered mentation or very high core temperature suggests heat stroke.

items.title: A client with heart failure gains 2.5 kg in 3 days and reports increasing orthopnea. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Notify provider promptly, assess congestion and oxygenation, review diuretic plan, and reinforce daily weights and symptom action plan.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Rapid weight gain and orthopnea suggest fluid retention and worsening heart failure.

items.title: A client reports sudden tearing chest/back pain with unequal arm blood pressures. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Activate emergency response, minimize exertion, monitor hemodynamics, and prepare prescribed IV beta blockade and urgent imaging.
items.rationale: Aortic dissection is a vascular emergency; reducing shear stress and rapid diagnosis are essential.

items.title: A client after cardiac surgery has hypotension, jugular venous distention, muffled heart sounds, and narrowing pulse pressure. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Cardiac tamponade|actions:Escalate immediately, support oxygenation and circulation, and prepare for urgent echocardiography/pericardial drainage.|evaluation:Beck triad and hemodynamic compromise suggest tamponade obstructing cardiac filling.
items.rationale: Beck triad and hemodynamic compromise suggest tamponade obstructing cardiac filling.

items.title: A client has irregular HR 158/min, BP 118/72 mm Hg, and palpitations without chest pain or syncope. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Assess stability, obtain ECG, notify provider, and prepare rate-control/anticoagulation decisions based on clinical context.
items.rationale: Stable AF with rapid ventricular response requires ECG confirmation and individualized rate/rhythm and stroke-risk management.

items.title: A monitored client becomes unresponsive, pulseless, and the rhythm is ventricular fibrillation. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Start CPR and defibrillate as soon as possible; follow ACLS and minimize interruptions.
items.rationale: VF is a shockable cardiac-arrest rhythm; early defibrillation and high-quality CPR improve survival.

items.title: A client has HR 34/min, BP 78/42 mm Hg, chest discomfort, and altered mentation. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Activate emergency response, support airway/circulation, prepare atropine and transcutaneous pacing per ACLS.
items.rationale: Bradycardia with hypotension and altered mentation is unstable and requires immediate intervention.

items.title: On postoperative day 1, a client has low-grade fever, diminished bases, and shallow respirations. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:On postoperative day 1, a client has low-grade fever, diminished bases, and shallow respirations.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Encourage early ambulation, upright positioning, deep breathing and incentive spirometry, and adequate analgesia.
items.rationale: Pain-related shallow breathing and immobility promote atelectasis; lung expansion and mobility help prevent it.

items.title: A client taking rifampin notices orange discoloration of urine and tears. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client taking rifampin notices orange discoloration of urine and tears.|response:Explain that orange-red body-fluid discoloration is expected, reinforce adherence, and review hepatotoxicity and drug interactions.|rationale:Rifampin commonly discolors body fluids; adherence and liver monitoring remain important.
items.rationale: Rifampin commonly discolors body fluids; adherence and liver monitoring remain important.

items.title: A client has frequent watery diarrhea after antibiotics and a positive C. difficile test. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:C. difficile infection|priority:Initiate contact precautions with soap-and-water hand hygiene, use sporicidal environmental cleaning, and administer prescribed therapy.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: C. difficile spores resist alcohol hand rub; contact precautions and soap-and-water reduce spread.

items.title: A hospitalized client has confirmed influenza with cough and fever. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Influenza isolation|actions:Use droplet precautions, appropriate mask and eye protection per policy, and encourage respiratory hygiene.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Influenza primarily spreads by respiratory droplets; follow facility-specific infection-control guidance.

items.title: A client 5 days after surgery has wound separation, purulent drainage, and fever. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client 5 days after surgery has wound separation, purulent drainage, and fever.|priority:Cover wound with sterile saline-moistened dressing if dehisced, notify surgeon, assess sepsis, and avoid reinserting exposed tissue.
items.rationale: Dehiscence/evisceration risk requires protection and urgent surgical evaluation.

items.title: A postoperative abdominal incision opens and bowel is visible. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Do not attempt to replace organs; moist sterile protection and urgent surgical care are essential.

items.title: Two hours after thyroidectomy, a client develops stridor and neck swelling. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Neck hematoma or laryngeal edema can rapidly obstruct the airway.

items.title: A client on postoperative day 3 has unilateral calf swelling, warmth, and tenderness. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Notify provider for urgent evaluation, avoid massaging the leg, and anticipate diagnostic ultrasound and anticoagulation if confirmed.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Unilateral swelling suggests DVT; massage may dislodge thrombus.

items.title: A client after hip replacement is reluctant to use sequential compression devices. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Explain purpose, apply devices correctly when in bed, encourage early ambulation, and administer prescribed prophylaxis.
items.rationale: Mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis reduce postoperative venous thromboembolism risk.

items.title: A client with iron-deficiency anemia reports fatigue and has microcytic indices and low ferritin. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Chronic anemia|actions:Administer prescribed iron, teach absorption strategies and expected dark stools/constipation, and investigate source of iron loss.|evaluation:Low ferritin and microcytosis support iron deficiency; replacement and cause evaluation are needed.
items.rationale: Low ferritin and microcytosis support iron deficiency; replacement and cause evaluation are needed.

items.title: A client with sickle cell disease has severe back and leg pain without fever or respiratory symptoms. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Assess pain and complications, provide prompt prescribed analgesia and hydration, and encourage incentive spirometry when appropriate.
items.rationale: Vaso-occlusive crisis requires timely analgesia and prevention of dehydration and acute chest syndrome.

items.title: A client with transfusion-dependent thalassemia receives regular packed RBCs and has elevated ferritin. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Monitor transfusion reactions and iron burden, reinforce chelation adherence, and trend cardiac/hepatic iron assessment.
items.rationale: Repeated transfusions cause iron overload; chelation prevents organ damage.

items.title: A child with hemophilia A has painful swollen knee after minor trauma. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Administer prescribed factor VIII promptly, rest/ice/elevate joint, and avoid IM injections and aspirin/NSAIDs unless specifically directed.
items.rationale: Early factor replacement prevents hemarthrosis-related joint damage.

items.title: A client with ANC 400 asks whether fresh flowers can be kept in the room. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client with ANC 400 asks whether fresh flowers can be kept in the room.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Follow facility protective-environment policy, avoid standing water/soil exposure, perform hand hygiene, and report fever immediately.
items.rationale: Soil and standing water can harbor organisms; neutropenic fever requires urgent action.

items.title: A client with platelets 18,000/mm³ has petechiae and gingival bleeding. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client with platelets 18,000/mm³ has petechiae and gingival bleeding.|response:Institute bleeding precautions, avoid IM/rectal procedures and NSAIDs, use soft oral care, and report active bleeding.|rationale:Severe thrombocytopenia increases spontaneous bleeding risk; minimize trauma.
items.rationale: Severe thrombocytopenia increases spontaneous bleeding risk; minimize trauma.

items.title: A septic client oozes from IV sites, has platelets 42,000/mm³, prolonged PT, and low fibrinogen. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Disseminated intravascular coagulation|priority:Treat underlying cause urgently, monitor bleeding/thrombosis and labs, and prepare blood component support as prescribed.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: DIC consumes platelets and clotting factors while causing microthrombi and bleeding.

items.title: During transfusion, an older client develops dyspnea, hypertension, crackles, and jugular venous distention. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Acute transfusion-associated circulatory overload|actions:Stop transfusion, sit upright, provide oxygen, notify provider/blood bank, and anticipate diuretic treatment.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: TACO is volume overload; respiratory support and diuresis are often required.

items.title: Within 2 hours of transfusion, a client develops acute hypoxemia, bilateral infiltrates, and hypotension without fluid overload. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:Within 2 hours of transfusion, a client develops acute hypoxemia, bilateral infiltrates, and hypotension without fluid overload.|priority:Stop transfusion, provide respiratory support, notify blood bank/provider, and report suspected TRALI.
items.rationale: TRALI causes noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and requires supportive care; diuretics are not routine absent overload.

items.title: A postpartum client reports hearing voices telling her to harm the infant. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency with risk of harm and requires immediate protection and treatment.

items.title: A client 3 weeks postpartum reports persistent sadness, guilt, and inability to enjoy usual activities but denies intent to self-harm. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Persistent symptoms beyond transient blues warrant assessment and treatment; safety questions are essential.

items.title: A 36-hour-old newborn has jaundice extending to the abdomen and poor feeding. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Obtain age-in-hours bilirubin assessment, evaluate feeding/hydration and hemolysis risk, and initiate phototherapy if threshold met.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Bilirubin treatment thresholds depend on age in hours and risk factors; early assessment prevents neurotoxicity.

items.title: A 2-day-old newborn has temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy, and apnea. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Escalate urgently, support airway/temperature/glucose, obtain cultures as ordered, and initiate prescribed empiric antibiotics promptly.
items.rationale: Neonatal infection may present subtly and progress rapidly; prompt stabilization and treatment are vital.

items.title: A caregiver plans to place a newborn prone on a soft pillow for sleep. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Safe sleep education|actions:Teach supine sleep on a firm, flat, separate surface without pillows, loose bedding, or soft objects.|evaluation:A safe sleep environment reduces sleep-related infant death risk.
items.rationale: A safe sleep environment reduces sleep-related infant death risk.

items.title: A caregiver asks how a newborn should ride home from the hospital. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Use a correctly installed rear-facing car seat in the back seat, following manufacturer height/weight limits.
items.rationale: Rear-facing positioning protects the infant's head, neck, and spine in a crash.

items.title: A breastfeeding parent reports severe nipple pain and a clicking sound during feeds. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Observe a full feed, assess latch and infant transfer, and refer to lactation support; correct shallow latch.
items.rationale: Persistent pain and clicking suggest ineffective latch and milk transfer.

items.title: A caregiver reports giving an adult teaspoon of liquid acetaminophen to a toddler. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Assess exact product, concentration, dose, time, and weight; contact poison control/provider as indicated and teach oral syringe use.
items.rationale: Liquid concentrations vary; dosing must be weight-based and measured with a calibrated device.

items.title: A parent says a child missed several routine vaccines and asks to restart the entire series. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A parent says a child missed several routine vaccines and asks to restart the entire series.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Use the current catch-up schedule; most vaccine series do not need restarting after extended intervals.
items.rationale: Catch-up schedules continue valid prior doses while respecting minimum ages and intervals.

items.title: A child with asthma uses rescue inhaler daily and wakes coughing several nights weekly. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A child with asthma uses rescue inhaler daily and wakes coughing several nights weekly.|response:Arrange prompt clinician review for poor control, reinforce controller adherence and spacer technique, and update written action plan.|rationale:Frequent rescue use and night symptoms indicate uncontrolled asthma and need treatment reassessment.
items.rationale: Frequent rescue use and night symptoms indicate uncontrolled asthma and need treatment reassessment.

items.title: A client treated for food-triggered anaphylaxis is preparing for discharge. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Anaphylaxis discharge teaching|priority:Teach epinephrine auto-injector use, carry two devices, activate emergency services after use, and arrange allergy follow-up.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Symptoms can recur after initial improvement; epinephrine is first-line and emergency evaluation is needed.

items.title: A client with diabetes has a foot ulcer probing to bone, fever, and elevated inflammatory markers. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Osteomyelitis|actions:Obtain cultures/imaging as ordered, assess perfusion and sepsis, and prepare prolonged targeted antimicrobial and source-control plan.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Deep ulcer with systemic signs raises concern for bone infection requiring multidisciplinary treatment.

items.title: A client has acute hot swollen knee, fever, and severe pain with passive movement. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client has acute hot swollen knee, fever, and severe pain with passive movement.|priority:Arrange urgent joint aspiration and cultures, notify provider, and prepare prompt antibiotics after cultures when feasible.
items.rationale: Septic arthritis can rapidly destroy cartilage and requires urgent drainage and antimicrobial treatment.

items.title: A client has sudden severe redness and pain at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Acute gout is inflammatory; diagnosis and treatment must consider infection and comorbidities.

items.title: After prolonged immobilization, a client has muscle pain, dark urine, and creatine kinase 12,000 U/L. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Myoglobin release can cause acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia; early hydration and monitoring are important.

items.title: After chemotherapy, a client has potassium 6.2, phosphate 6.5, uric acid 11, and calcium 7.1 mg/dL. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Escalate urgently, institute cardiac monitoring, administer prescribed hydration and urate-lowering therapy, and trend electrolytes/renal function.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Rapid tumor breakdown releases intracellular electrolytes and uric acid, risking dysrhythmia and renal failure.

items.title: A client with lung cancer develops facial/neck swelling, distended neck veins, and dyspnea worse when supine. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Elevate head, assess airway/oxygenation, notify oncology team urgently, and avoid upper-extremity venipuncture when possible.
items.rationale: Venous obstruction can compromise airway and cerebral venous drainage.

items.title: A client with metastatic cancer reports new severe back pain, leg weakness, and urinary retention. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Spinal cord compression|actions:Treat as oncologic emergency, notify provider immediately, maintain spinal precautions as indicated, and prepare urgent MRI/corticosteroid/radiation evaluation.|evaluation:New motor and sphincter deficits may signal cord compression; delay risks permanent paralysis.
items.rationale: New motor and sphincter deficits may signal cord compression; delay risks permanent paralysis.

items.title: A neutropenic client after chemotherapy has fever, right lower quadrant pain, and diarrhea. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Escalate urgently, keep NPO, obtain cultures/imaging as ordered, and prepare broad-spectrum antibiotics and supportive care.
items.rationale: Typhlitis can progress to perforation and sepsis in profound neutropenia.

items.title: A client with multiple myeloma has headache, blurred vision, mucosal bleeding, and confusion. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Notify hematology urgently, assess neurologic/visual status, and prepare for prescribed plasmapheresis.
items.rationale: Hyperviscosity impairs microcirculation and can cause neurologic, visual, and bleeding symptoms.

items.title: A client with multiple myeloma has rising creatinine and hypercalcemia. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Monitor renal function, hydration, calcium, and nephrotoxic exposures; administer prescribed therapy and avoid dehydration.
items.rationale: Light chains, hypercalcemia, and volume depletion contribute to myeloma-associated kidney injury.

items.title: A client after stroke coughs with thin liquids and has a wet voice. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client after stroke coughs with thin liquids and has a wet voice.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Keep NPO until swallow evaluation, provide oral care, and use recommended consistency and positioning after assessment.
items.rationale: Dysphagia increases aspiration pneumonia risk; texture modification should follow formal assessment.

items.title: An intubated client is receiving mechanical ventilation. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:An intubated client is receiving mechanical ventilation.|response:Maintain head-of-bed elevation when not contraindicated, oral care per protocol, daily sedation/ventilator liberation assessment, and hand hygiene.|rationale:Evidence-based ventilator care reduces aspiration and duration of ventilation.
items.rationale: Evidence-based ventilator care reduces aspiration and duration of ventilation.

items.title: A septic client has severe hypoxemia despite oxygen, bilateral opacities, and no evidence of cardiac failure. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:ARDS|priority:Escalate critical care, anticipate lung-protective ventilation with appropriate PEEP, and monitor oxygenation/hemodynamics.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: ARDS causes noncardiogenic pulmonary edema; lung-protective ventilation limits ventilator-induced injury.

items.title: A mechanically ventilated client with severe ARDS remains hypoxemic despite optimized ventilation. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Prone positioning|actions:Prepare for prolonged prone positioning by securing airway/lines, protecting pressure points, and coordinating trained team.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Proning can improve ventilation-perfusion matching in severe ARDS and requires meticulous safety checks.

items.title: A ventilated client is awake, hemodynamically stable, has improving cause of failure, and adequate oxygenation. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A ventilated client is awake, hemodynamically stable, has improving cause of failure, and adequate oxygenation.|priority:Collaborate on spontaneous breathing trial readiness, assess cough/secretions and airway protection, and monitor trial tolerance.
items.rationale: Extubation requires more than oxygenation; mental status, airway protection, and secretion burden matter.

items.title: A client with a tracheostomy develops distress and no airflow through the tube. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Mucus plugging can obstruct the artificial airway; rapid patency assessment and oxygenation are critical.

items.title: A fresh tracheostomy placed yesterday becomes dislodged. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: A fresh tract can create a false passage; reinsertion requires experienced personnel and emergency planning.

items.title: A young adult reports chest pain and agitation after cocaine use; BP 188/110 mm Hg. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Obtain ECG, monitor for ischemia/dysrhythmia, reduce sympathetic stimulation with prescribed benzodiazepine, and follow ACS evaluation.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Cocaine increases myocardial oxygen demand and vasoconstriction; benzodiazepines help control adrenergic excess.

items.title: A client has BP 224/128 mm Hg with acute confusion and retinal hemorrhages. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Activate emergency response, assess end-organ injury, establish monitoring, and administer titratable IV antihypertensive as prescribed.
items.rationale: Severe BP with acute target-organ damage is a hypertensive emergency requiring controlled reduction.

items.title: An older adult becomes dizzy when standing; BP falls from 138/78 supine to 104/62 standing. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Orthostatic hypotension|actions:Assist to sit/lie down, assess volume and medications, teach slow position changes, and use fall precautions.|evaluation:A symptomatic orthostatic drop increases fall risk and may reflect medication or volume issues.
items.rationale: A symptomatic orthostatic drop increases fall risk and may reflect medication or volume issues.

items.title: A client briefly loses consciousness while standing and has palpitations before the event. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Assess ABCs, ECG, orthostatic vitals, glucose, and injury; escalate if cardiac symptoms or abnormal findings.
items.rationale: Syncope with palpitations may indicate dysrhythmia and requires cardiac evaluation.

items.title: An older adult with exertional syncope has a harsh systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Assess hemodynamic stability, avoid exertion, and arrange prompt cardiac evaluation; report syncope urgently.
items.rationale: Classic symptoms of severe aortic stenosis include angina, syncope, and dyspnea.

items.title: A client with a prosthetic valve has fever, new murmur, and positive blood cultures. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Obtain ordered cultures before antibiotics when feasible, monitor embolic/heart-failure signs, and administer prolonged IV antimicrobials as prescribed.
items.rationale: Prosthetic valve endocarditis carries high complication risk and requires organism-directed therapy.

items.title: A client has sharp chest pain relieved by leaning forward and diffuse ST elevation. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client has sharp chest pain relieved by leaning forward and diffuse ST elevation.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Assess hemodynamics and ECG, notify provider, and administer prescribed anti-inflammatory treatment; monitor for tamponade.
items.rationale: Positional pleuritic pain and diffuse ST changes suggest pericarditis; tamponade is a critical complication.

items.title: A client after myocardial infarction asks when to resume exercise. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client after myocardial infarction asks when to resume exercise.|response:Follow individualized cardiac rehabilitation plan, begin graded activity after clearance, and stop/report chest pain, syncope, or disproportionate dyspnea.|rationale:Supervised progression improves recovery while monitoring for ischemic symptoms.
items.rationale: Supervised progression improves recovery while monitoring for ischemic symptoms.

items.title: A client has calf pain with walking relieved by rest, diminished pulses, and cool feet. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Peripheral arterial disease|priority:Promote supervised walking, smoking cessation, foot care, and prescribed antiplatelet/statin therapy; report rest pain or tissue loss.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Intermittent claudication reflects arterial insufficiency; risk-factor management and exercise improve function.

items.title: A client has bilateral ankle edema, brown lower-leg discoloration, and shallow irregular ulcers near the medial malleoli. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Venous insufficiency|actions:Assess arterial perfusion before compression, elevate legs, support compression therapy if appropriate, and provide wound care.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Venous hypertension causes edema and gaiter-area ulcers; compression is used only after arterial status is assessed.

items.title: A client has arm swelling on the side of axillary node dissection. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client has arm swelling on the side of axillary node dissection.|priority:Encourage prescribed compression/exercise and skin care, avoid trauma, and report redness/fever; follow individualized limb precautions.
items.rationale: Lymphatic disruption causes swelling and infection risk; evidence-based lymphedema care supports drainage and function.

items.title: A client develops sudden severe eye pain, halos, headache, nausea, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Acute angle-closure glaucoma threatens vision and requires immediate reduction of intraocular pressure.
